newsitem.title: USA: US High Court upholds rule for patent cases.
newsitem.headline: US High Court upholds rule for patent cases.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Monday in upholding a key part of patent law that makes it easier for patent holders to protect their inventions from similar ideas.
The high court upheld what has been known since 1950 as the so-called "doctrine of equivalents."

Under the doctrine, a product or process that does not literally infringe upon the express terms of a patent may still be found to infringe it if there is an "equivalence" between the elements of one item and the patented invention.

Justice Clarence Thomas wrote for the high court that a number of factors must go into the doctrine's application, including the patent's context and the particular circumstances of the case. "The determination of equivalence should be applied as an objective inquiry on an element-by-element basis," he said. The court did not address whether application of the doctrine must be done by the judge or jury.

The ruling was a defeat for Warner-Jenkinson Co, a subsidiary of Universal Foods Corp, in a case against Hilton Davis Chemical Co, a unit of Philadelphia-based Freedom Chemical Co. The two companies had similar approaches for a process to remove impurities from red and yellow food dyes.
